baseProblem.statement: Given an array of integers and a target value, return the indices of the two numbers that add up to the target. Each input has exactly one solution, and you cannot use the same element twice.

rounds.question: What structure lets each element find its complement in O(1)?

options.conceptLabel: A sorted copy of the array
options.rationale: Sorting enables a two-pointer scan but costs O(n log n) and forces you to carry original indices through the sort — slower and more error-prone than a hash lookup.

options.conceptLabel: A hash map from value to its index
options.rationale: Storing each value's index lets you check in O(1) whether the complement you need has already appeared — the heart of the one-pass solution.

options.conceptLabel: A set of values seen so far
options.rationale: A set tells you the complement exists but not WHERE. The problem asks for indices, so you must map value to index.

options.conceptLabel: A running total of the elements
options.rationale: An aggregate sum is irrelevant — Two Sum is about pairwise complements, not a cumulative total.

rounds.question: With the value-to-index map ready, how do you scan so you hold both the value and its index?

options.conceptLabel: Enumerate to get index and value together
options.rationale: You must return the index, so iterate with both the position and the value in hand.

options.conceptLabel: Iterate over the values only
options.rationale: Without the index you cannot report WHERE the pair is — and the contract asks for indices, not values.

options.conceptLabel: Two nested loops over every pair

fragments.python:
for i in range(len(nums)):
            for j in range(i + 1, len(nums)):
fragments.java: for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) for (int j = i + 1; j < nums.length; j++) {

options.rationale: The brute-force O(n^2) double loop works but throws away the whole point of the hash map — one pass suffices.

options.conceptLabel: Walk two pointers inward from both ends

fragments.python:
lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1
        while lo < hi:
fragments.java: int lo = 0, hi = nums.length - 1; while (lo < hi) {

options.rationale: Two-pointer needs a SORTED array; on the raw input the ends have no ordering relationship, so it can't reliably find the pair.

rounds.question: Enumerating gives you each value x and its index. What value completes the pair with x?

options.conceptLabel: x itself
options.rationale: Looking up x finds x, not its partner — you'd try to pair an element with a copy of itself.

options.conceptLabel: target plus x
options.rationale: Addition overshoots: you want two numbers that SUM to target, so the partner is target minus x.

options.conceptLabel: target minus x, the complement
options.rationale: If x + y = target then y = target - x, so the complement is exactly what completes the pair.

options.conceptLabel: target minus twice x
options.rationale: This is right only when the two numbers are equal; in general it computes the wrong partner.

rounds.question: You can now compute the complement need. In what order do you check seen and store x?

options.conceptLabel: Store x first, then check for the complement

fragments.java:
seen.put(nums[i], i);
            if (seen.containsKey(need)) return new int[]{seen.get(need), i};

options.rationale: Storing before checking lets an element match itself when need == x, violating 'cannot use the same element twice'.

options.conceptLabel: Check for the complement first, then store x

fragments.java:
if (seen.containsKey(need)) return new int[]{seen.get(need), i};
            seen.put(nums[i], i);

options.rationale: Checking before inserting guarantees the match is with an EARLIER element, so you never reuse the same index.

options.conceptLabel: Only store; never check inside the loop
options.rationale: If you merely build the map you never detect the pair — the loop finishes having found nothing.

options.conceptLabel: Append x to a result list
options.rationale: Collecting values doesn't test the pair condition; it just copies the input.

rounds.question: The loop returns the pair as soon as it finds it. Given one guaranteed solution, what's the fallback return?

options.conceptLabel: An empty list — the not-found fallback
options.rationale: The guarantee means the loop returns early; an empty list is the conventional 'no pair' sentinel if it ever falls through.

options.conceptLabel: The seen map
options.rationale: Returning the lookup table leaks internals and isn't the index pair the contract requires.

options.conceptLabel: The last index
options.rationale: A lone index is meaningless — the answer is a PAIR of indices.

options.conceptLabel: Null / None
options.rationale: A null sentinel forces every caller to guard a case the problem says can't happen; an empty list is cleaner.

lightning.question: Your one-pass hashmap solution — time and extra space?
options: O(n log n) time, O(n) space
lightning.explanation: One scan with O(1) expected map operations is O(n) time, but the map can end up holding almost every number — O(n) space is the price of the speed.

lightning.question: Why does storing each number AFTER checking for its complement matter for nums=[3, 3], target=6?
options: It doesn't — the order is a style choice
It avoids overwriting the target value
It stops a number from pairing with itself while still letting two equal values pair
lightning.explanation: Check-then-store means the second 3 finds the first 3 already in the map, but a lone 3 can never match itself — store-first would return [0, 0] for a single 3 with target 6.

lightning.question: Follow-up: the array is already sorted. Which approach gives O(n) time with O(1) extra space?
options: Two pointers walking inward from both ends
Binary search for each element's complement
lightning.explanation: Sorted input unlocks the two-pointer walk: sum too small → move lo, too big → move hi. O(n) time, no map. Binary search per element works but costs O(n log n).
